extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policy makers, and agency officials interested in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and normative criteria for how agencies conduct informal notice-and-comment rulemaking and how public comments should be treated and weighted. Focuses on procedural requirements, participation patterns, comment quality, e-rulemaking effects, and agency responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §553 notice-and-comment requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must publish advance notice and take public comment prior to finalizing a legally binding rule (section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As interpreted by courts, agencies also must publicly disclose the data on which they rely prior to seeking comment and must explain their reasons for rejecting significant comments (citing ACLU v. FCC; United States v. Nova Scotia Food Prods. Corp.; Portland Cement Ass’n v. Ruckelshaus). These requirements codify an entitlement to public participation and some public reason-giving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review for reasoned decisions (5 U.S.C. §706)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may vacate an agency decision if it is not reasoned, does not follow substantive legal requirements in the authorizing statute or the APA, or is arbitrary or capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard ensures agencies are accountable for following law and gives courts a mechanism to enforce explanation and reasoned decisionmaking; it is part of what makes rulemaking procedurally meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation balance in public participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual participation in rulemaking is often not well balanced: regulated entities tend to be heavily represented compared with regulatory beneficiaries or ordinary citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies (e.g., Wagner; Yackee & Yackee; Golden) show business/regulatory interests often submit the majority of comments in many rulemakings; exceptions occur for high-salience rules where lay public comments predominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and barriers to participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation is not cost-free: it takes resources to discover a rulemaking, understand the issues, and prepare persuasive comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of free-rider problems and resource constraints, diffuse regulatory beneficiaries and ordinary citizens face substantial impediments to participating; this affects who can effectively engage in rulemaking (citing Federal E-Rulemaking Report; Olson; Schlozman & Tierney).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information asymmetry and control by regulated entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulated entities often possess greater control of certain types of information (e.g., costs, feasibility) that are especially valuable to agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can make agencies particularly attentive to regulated-entity comments; regulated parties can also deluge agencies with information, potentially crowding out other views (citing Wagner; Yackee & Yackee).

rubrics_metrics.name: E-rulemaking's mixed effects on participation
rubrics_metrics.description: E-rulemaking may reduce some participation imbalances by lowering the cost of identifying proposed rules and submitting comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, for already high-visibility rulemakings it may simply increase the size of the 'bounce' (more submissions) without broadening the range of interests represented; it also enables possibilities like commenting on others' comments (citing Federal E-Rulemaking Report; Coglianese; Noveck).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency responsiveness favors technical/sophisticated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies appear to treat technically and scientifically oriented comments more seriously than value-laden or policy-focused comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work (Cuéllar and others) suggests sophisticated comments—often from organized groups—receive more attention and response from agencies, even when they do not mention the full range of lay concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a 'sophisticated' comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophisticated comments reveal awareness of statutory constraints, provide concrete examples or discrete logical arguments, and supply legal, policy, or empirical background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cuéllar added two further markers: inclusion of a paragraph interpreting the statutory requirement and proposing an explicit change in the regulation. Such comments are more likely to get agency attention and response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of layperson comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments from individual laypersons often raise concerns that are relevant to the agency's legal mandate, ranging from personal experience to policy preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some comments may be legally out-of-bounds under particular statutes, the broad phrasing of many statutes means most lay comments in studies were indeed relevant (examples provided from EPA rule comments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency treatment of mass submissions and form letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass submissions (form letters, postcards, identical e-mails) are frequently treated perfunctorily or derided by agency staff and may not be analyzed as if they were votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies often note large numbers but give detailed responses primarily to more technical or non-duplicative comments; they may not track duplicates and sometimes explicitly avoid treating input as a vote (examples: FCC, Forest Service, BLM, NPS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies must provide reasoned responses to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are obliged, under judicial interpretation, to explain their reasons for accepting or rejecting significant comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide adequate engagement with significant comments undermines a democratic vision of rulemaking; examples show agencies sometimes fail to respond (e.g., CPSC infant bath seats) while other agencies give brief or minimal rationales (e.g., FAA on wing fittings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cloaking policy choices in scientific terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies frequently 'cloak' resolution of value or policy questions in scientific or technical framing, making it harder to see value choices explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters and scholars note that 'agency science . . . is laced with policy decisions at numerous levels'; transparency requires explicit acknowledgment of normative choices rather than burying them in technical determinations (citing Meazell; Wagner).
